tldr: When transferring dexterous human hand tasks to a robot, reproducing contact force matters just as much as matching kinematic poses. This paper presents ReForce, a method that captures both. Trained on large-scale simulation, a general force-tracking policy makes fine real-time adjustments to joint commands using fingertip force feedback. Real-robot experiments show it can grasp delicate objects, like a paper cup, without crushing or dropping them.
hero_caption: Overview of ReForce. Human hand motions and fingertip contact forces are captured simultaneously. The policy predicts an online correction on top of the kinematically retargeted command. This prevents slippage and insufficient contact force seen in conventional kinematics-only retargeting, enabling stable, contact-rich manipulation.
overview:
Human demonstrations offer a scalable data source for teaching dexterous multi-finger manipulation to robots. However, humans and robot hands differ fundamentally in their embodiment, including finger lengths, joint layouts, and stiffness. This creates an embodiment gap that requires "retargeting" human motions into robot joint angles. Traditional retargeting predominantly relies on kinematic approaches that match joint geometry alone. Yet manipulation is decided by force. Too much force crushes the object; too little lets it slip away.

Recent attempts use reinforcement learning in simulation to reproduce forces, but they require high-fidelity 3D models (digital twins) for each object or fail to run during online teleoperation. To overcome these hurdles, this paper presents ReForce, a general force tracker that reproduces desired contact forces using online fingertip force feedback without requiring prior object models.

ReForce is trained via imitation learning on diverse hand-object contact data collected in large-scale simulation. On the real robot, it operates in a closed loop, predicting and adding a small correction (residual) to kinematically computed joint commands to bridge the gap between desired and measured fingertip contact forces. Evaluated on a robot arm with a 12-DoF dexterous hand on tasks like grasping fragile paper cups and operating spring-loaded tongs, ReForce significantly reduced force-tracking errors and achieved solid multi-finger contact compared to conventional admittance control or position replay, across both real hardware and simulation.
contributions: Proposed a new framework that dynamically corrects kinematic retargeting via online fingertip force feedback without requiring a digital twin of the target object beforehand.
Constructed post-hoc contact targets from large-scale simulation contact data to train a single, general force-tracking policy.

Supported both online teleoperation and offline data translation (action and force chunking via ACT), demonstrating effectiveness on contact-critical real-world tasks like grasping paper cups and squeezing tongs.

sections.heading: Matching hand poses is not enough: Moving toward force-aware retargeting
sections.summary: Transferring human demonstrations to multi-finger hands is hard due to physical embodiment differences. Existing kinematic retargeting only matches poses while ignoring forces, leading to grasp failures or broken objects during contact tasks. This work introduces ReForce, which reproduces intended contact forces using online force feedback without relying on prior object models.
sections.details:
Human demonstrations are key to scaling dexterous manipulation in robotics, but robot hands differ significantly from human hands in geometry and joint structures—an embodiment gap. Most retargeting methods today are kinematic, using optimization to geometrically align human and robot joint positions. However, purely geometric alignment ignores object shapes and contact dynamics, resulting in only coarse motion matching. In practice, practitioners must either retrain policies on robot-collected data or have human teleoperators visually and intuitively compensate for the discrepancy.

Yet the essence of manipulation lies in force. Whether contact forces are appropriate dictates whether an object is securely held, crushed, or dropped. Recent studies have explored simulation-based force-aware retargeting, but these assume exact digital twins (high-precision CAD models and pose estimates) of both the hand and object, rendering them impractical for novel items. Moreover, because they optimize entire trajectories offline, they cannot support real-time teleoperation, which is crucial for collecting high-quality demonstrations.

To address these limitations, this paper proposes a general force-tracking approach. By collecting diverse contact data in simulation, the authors train a closed-loop force tracker that predicts and adds a real-time residual to kinematically derived joint commands. This approach eliminates the need for digital twins and achieves zero-shot, well-modulated contact in both online teleoperation and offline data translation.

sections.heading: At the crossroads of imitation learning, dexterous retargeting, and tactile control
sections.summary: This section reviews prior work in learning from human demonstrations, multi-finger retargeting, and tactile/force feedback control. ReForce sits as an execution layer that takes human motion and force intent and locally adapts the robot's motion based on real-time contact feedback from the hardware.
sections.details:
Related work spans three primary domains:

- Learning from human demonstrations:
Advances in imitation learning and large datasets have accelerated the generation of robot trajectories from human demonstrations. Particularly in contact-rich tasks, demonstrations convey not just geometric movements, but contact skills themselves. ReForce builds on this perspective, adapting human-derived trajectories whenever the robot's measured fingertip forces diverge from the intended contacts in the demo.

- Dexterous multi-finger retargeting:
To bridge structural gaps between humans and robots, prior work has explored teleoperation systems, motion capture, and RL-based residual corrections. However, most focus on mapping human motions into robot joint spaces. In contrast, ReForce tackles how the robot should dynamically react to real-time contact feedback given motion and force references.

- Force and tactile feedback for contact-rich manipulation:
Classical hybrid position/force control and admittance control (which maps force errors to displacement via virtual spring-damper dynamics) enable compliance against contact, but require manual per-task tuning of gains and mappings. Recent visuo-tactile policies also perform well, yet typically remain confined to single, specific tasks. ReForce preserves the low-latency local feedback benefits of classical control while providing a learned, flexible retargeting controller compatible with various reference inputs.

sections.heading: How to build a general force tracker trained in simulation
sections.summary: ReForce is a closed-loop policy that predicts minor joint command residuals from joint angles and 5-finger contact force errors. It is trained via behavioral cloning on post-hoc targets derived from diverse simulated contact interactions, and pairs with a higher-level ACT policy to track motion and force reference trajectories.
sections.details:
3.1 Problem formulation:
Let $q_{t}^{\mathrm{obs}} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_{q}}$ be the observed joint angles of the robot hand at time $t$, and let $F_{t} \in \mathbb{R}^{5}$ denote the normal forces measured at the five fingertips (thumb, index, middle, ring, pinky). A higher-level reference source provides target joint angles $q_{t}^{\star}$ and target contact forces $F_{t}^{\star}$. The policy inputs are normalized features containing the current state, target state, and their tracking errors ($q_{t}^{\star}-q_{t}^{\mathrm{obs}}$ and $F_{t}^{\star}-F_{t}$). The ReForce policy $\theta$ outputs bounded joint command increments, which are clipped within joint limits $[q_{\min}, q_{\max}]$ and accumulated into command values $q_{t}^{\mathrm{cmd}}$ sent to the robot.

3.2 Policy training and post-hoc targets:
The policy is trained on simulated interaction data covering random hand poses and object contact properties. A key design is post-hoc target creation: median joint angles and forces over a future time window of $K_{t}$ steps are set as targets $q_{t}^{\star}, F_{t}^{\star}$, while the single-step demo action $\Delta q_{t}^{\mathrm{demo}} = q_{t+1}-q_{t}$ serves as the supervision label. Learning uses a behavioral cloning loss that computes mean squared error per joint and averages it equally across fingers. This naturally teaches the policy recovery behaviors against contact timing offsets and missed contacts.

3.3 Learning from human demonstrations and integration:
Human hand motions and fingertip FSR sensor readings are calibrated into the robot reference space. To imitate these references, a reference policy based on ACT (Action Chunking with Transformers) is trained. ACT predicts short future chunks of joint targets and intended forces from joint history and task phase. Crucially, ACT does not receive real-time force feedback; it only predicts phase-dependent contact intent, leaving all closed-loop dynamic adjustments to the lower-level ReForce tracker in a decoupled, hierarchical design.

captions.F2: ReForce training and inference pipeline. (a) During training, post-hoc targets are constructed over a future window from simulation interactions to train the force tracker via behavioral cloning. (b) During deployment, the policy uses fingertip tactile feedback to apply online corrections $\Delta q_{\mathrm{cmd}}$ to motion and force reference trajectories supplied by human demonstrations or ACT.

sections.heading: Real-world tests: Balancing gentle forces with solid contact
sections.summary: ReForce was evaluated on a real robot arm with a multi-finger hand on paper-cup grasping and tongs manipulation tasks. Compared to naive position replay and classical admittance control, it achieved lower force-tracking error, prevented dropped contacts, and boosted task success rates within safe force limits.
sections.details:
4.1 Real-robot experimental setup:
The hardware platform comprises a UFACTORY xArm and a 12-DoF XHand equipped with fingertip tactile sensors. Teleoperation uses a VR controller (wrist pose), a Manus glove (finger joints), and calibrated fingertip FSR sensors (contact forces), normalizing human and robot forces to a shared Newton scale. The evaluation tasks were paper-cup grasping (fragile, force threshold 1.0 N) and tongs manipulation (spring-loaded, force threshold 3.0 N).

4.1.1 Replay of recorded trajectories:
When replaying the same human demonstration trajectories, ReForce achieved lower force-tracking errors (mean absolute error) in both side and top grasps compared to direct replay and classical admittance control (hand-tuned spring-damper mapping). Direct replay frequently missed contact even after reaching target positions, while admittance control tended to leave residual force when contact should have been unloaded. ReForce smoothly adapted both contact establishment and release.

4.1.2 Integration with learned reference policy (ACT):
When tracking target trajectories generated by ACT, ReForce scored the highest safe success rate, the lowest force-tracking error, and zero instances of severe contact disengagement (defined as 3 or more fingers losing contact) on the paper cup task, engaging the highest average number of fingers. On tongs manipulation, admittance control had a slight edge in force error, but ReForce still drastically reduced contact disengagements over the standalone reference policy, maintaining secure multi-finger contact.

4.2 Simulation ablation study:
The team analyzed training data composition and policy inputs across 14,605 simulated episodes. Adding the target joint angles $q^{\star}$ to the inputs cut force tracking error by about 32–35%, and including explicit error features ($q^{\star}-q^{\mathrm{obs}}$ and $F^{\star}-F$) improved precision even further. Moreover, augmenting the training mix with reference-stall data (20%, simulating frozen reference poses) and pose-drift data (10%, perturbing finger joints toward limits under low force) alongside base data (70%) yielded the lowest force-tracking error overall (0.0379 ± 0.0006 N).

captions.F3: System setup for real-robot experiments and demonstration collection. A VR controller, tactile glove, and fingertip FSR sensors capture human hand motion and contact forces, which are retargeted to the xArm and XHand robot platform.
captions.F4: Behavioral comparison across methods during paper-cup grasping. Position control (direct replay) suffers from disengaged contact, and admittance control maintains unwanted residual force, whereas ReForce achieves both proper contact engagement and safe unloading.
captions.F5: Dataset mixing ratio used in simulation ablations. Combining standard data (Base: 70%) with reference-stall augmentations (20%) and pose-drift augmentations (10%) improves recovery from contact misalignments.

sections.heading: Looking ahead: Expanding to visual perception and shear forces
sections.summary: ReForce acts as a force-aware execution layer between kinematic references and robot hardware, enhancing contact-rich dexterous manipulation. Future directions include integrating camera observations for environmental perception and leveraging shear forces and slip information alongside normal forces.
sections.details:
This work presented ReForce, a retargeting method that dynamically adapts human motion and force references using online fingertip force feedback. Real-robot experiments proved that it significantly enhances force tracking fidelity and multi-finger contact engagement in contact-sensitive manipulation tasks.

Nonetheless, the authors point out two primary limitations of the current system:

- Lack of visual perception:
The higher-level ACT reference policy relies strictly on joint angle history and task execution phase, leaving it unable to adapt to unexpected object shifts or environmental changes. Feeding visual inputs such as camera streams into the policy would enable generating robust motion and force references grounded in the scene state.

- Restricted tactile modalities:
ReForce currently tracks only normal contact forces at the fingertips. However, sophisticated manipulation heavily relies on shear forces (friction), slip detection, and pressure distributions across the contact surface. Incorporating these richer tactile signals into the control loop represents a promising avenue for future development.

sections.heading: Appendix: Data normalization and real-robot force profiles
sections.summary: Details on the log-transformation used to normalize force inputs for stable training, along with per-finger force-tracking profiles recorded during real-robot evaluations.
sections.details:
To achieve stable tracking during real-robot deployment, special care was given to input feature normalization. While joint angles are standardized using training set means and standard deviations, contact forces follow a heavily skewed, long-tailed distribution concentrated near zero with a wide positive tail. Consequently, forces are first transformed via a logarithm: $F_{\log} = \log(1 + F / s_F)$ (with scale parameter $s_F = 1.0$ N), and then standardized with mean $\mu_F$ and standard deviation $\sigma_F$. This preprocessing allows the network to learn both subtle contact onsets near zero and substantial grasp forces with high precision.

Examining time-series force profiles during real-robot paper-cup grasps (both top and side grasps) reveals that direct replay sometimes fails to touch the object entirely, whereas admittance control exhibits persistent residual force long after the target drops to zero. In contrast, ReForce closely tracks both the rising and falling edges of the reference profile, verifying that all fingers maintain balanced contact throughout manipulation.

captions.F6: Per-finger contact force profiles during real-robot paper cup grasps from the top (left) and side (right). ReForce (red) closely follows the rising and falling edges of the target (purple), resolving issues like missed contacts in position replay (gray) and residual force in admittance control (cyan).

takeaways: Incorporating force feedback into retargeting prevents both loose, missed contacts and crushing forces caused by embodiment gaps.
Without building digital twins, a practical, force-adaptive policy can be pre-trained purely on large-scale simulation contact data using post-hoc targets.

Decoupling the architecture—letting the high-level policy (e.g., ACT) predict contact intent without a closed force loop, while a low-level tracker handles dynamic force adjustments—proves highly practical.
Because contact forces exhibit long-tailed distributions, log-transforming them before normalization is effective for stabilizing policy training.
limitations: The reference generation policy lacks visual perception, preventing it from adapting to object displacements or significant geometric changes.
The system relies solely on normal forces from fingertip sensors, without utilizing richer tactile cues like shear forces, slip, or contact torques.
Occasional over-force trials were observed in certain tasks requiring continuous modulation, such as tongs manipulation.
